projects.title: TCG Signal
projects.summary: Price and set guide for Pokémon card collectors. React front end served from Cloudflare; an ASP.NET Core API and a separate inventory service run in Cloudflare Containers over PostgreSQL.
outcomes: Scheduled jobs record daily prices into PostgreSQL, which power price history and market movers.
The set advisor falls back to a rule-based summary when the AI provider is unavailable.
One Cloudflare Worker serves the static front end and routes /api to the containers; Neon PostgreSQL for data.

projects.title: Freight Ops
projects.summary: Standalone freight CRM: customer accounts, a ranked opportunity queue, an operational dashboard, and read-only external load visibility. Built as a companion to LTL Planner and Yard Ops, covering the customer side of the same freight workflow.
outcomes: Explainable opportunity scoring: every account gets a priority score, the reason behind it, and a suggested next action.
Optional read-only Alvys load search through a server-side OAuth client-credentials adapter; falls back to synthetic data by default.
Runs on its own with Docker Compose on synthetic data; deploys to Cloudflare Workers + Containers from GitHub Actions.
projects.note: Clean-room project built from general domain knowledge on synthetic data. It is not employer code and contains no employer data, schemas, or screens.

projects.title: LTL Planner
projects.summary: Standalone LTL planning app that groups shipment orders onto compatible trucks under pallet, weight, and equipment limits, and explains every assignment it makes. Built to work in tandem with Yard Ops through a signed, versioned HTTP contract.
outcomes: Hard constraints (equipment, pallets, weight) filter trucks before any scoring; each planned truck carries a plain-language explanation.
Works in tandem with Yard Ops: serves trailer-fit candidates and ingests HMAC-signed Yard events idempotently by event ID, rejecting unknown schema versions.
Runs on its own with Docker Compose on synthetic data; deploys to Cloudflare Workers + Containers from GitHub Actions.
projects.note: Clean-room project built from general domain knowledge on synthetic data. It is not employer code and contains no employer data, schemas, or screens.

projects.title: Yard Ops
projects.summary: Standalone yard execution app: yard board, gate in/out, and dock inspections in a tablet-friendly UI. Built to work in tandem with LTL Planner, and still fully usable when the planner is offline.
outcomes: Works in tandem with LTL Planner: looks up planning candidates synchronously and sends state changes as HMAC-signed events.
Yard actions commit locally first; an outbox retries delivery to the planner with bounded exponential backoff.
Runs on its own with Docker Compose on synthetic data; deploys to Cloudflare Workers + Containers from GitHub Actions.

projects.title: WorkLens
projects.summary: Self-hosted job feed and application tracker: ASP.NET Core API over SQL Server with an Angular front end, run locally with Docker Compose.
outcomes: Clean Architecture backend with Core, Infrastructure, and API projects; EF Core migrations applied against a real SQL Server in CI.
Job feed from RemoteOK, Remotive, the Greenhouse Job Board API, and Dice’s Job Search MCP server, refreshed by a background service.
Application pipeline, follow-up reminders, analytics, a browser extension, Outlook sync through Microsoft Graph, and OpenAI-assisted resume matching.

publicRepos.name: Allocation Proration
publicRepos.description: Pro-rates a limited investment allocation across investors by historical average, redistributing whatever capped investors can’t take

layers.name: React UI
layers.note: Form and results, served as static assets

layers.name: Proration core
layers.note: Pure function, no dependencies, fully unit-tested

decisions.choice: The allocation math as a pure, dependency-free function
decisions.why: The algorithm is the part that has to be right: it caps investors at their request and keeps redistributing the remainder until nothing is left. Isolating it means every edge case (zero history, everyone capped, duplicate names, a “__proto__” investor) is a fast unit test rather than an HTTP test.

decisions.choice: One Cloudflare Worker serving both the UI and the API
decisions.instead: a separate static host and API server
decisions.why: One deployable, one origin (so no CORS), and no server to keep warm. Input limits on investor count and amounts keep the per-request work bounded, which matters on a platform that bills by CPU time.

publicRepos.name: Clean Architecture
publicRepos.description: CQRS/MediatR Clean Architecture reference — the same Core/Infrastructure/API boundary I’ve shipped at Kenworth, Global Holdings, and in WorkLens

layers.name: Domain
layers.note: Entities, value objects, domain events — no outward dependencies

layers.name: Application
layers.note: CQRS handlers, validation, mapping, interfaces Infrastructure implements

layers.name: Infrastructure
layers.note: EF Core, Identity, file export, external services

layers.name: WebUI
layers.note: ASP.NET Core API + Angular client, wires it together via DI

decisions.choice: CQRS with MediatR for every use case
decisions.instead: a conventional service layer with multi-purpose service classes
decisions.why: Each handler stays single-purpose and testable in isolation, and cross-cutting concerns (validation, logging, performance, authorization) attach as pipeline behaviours instead of being re-implemented per method. I default to this once a domain has more than a handful of use cases; for a 3-endpoint CRUD app the pipeline machinery isn’t worth it.

decisions.instead: a generic IRepository<T> wrapper over EF Core
decisions.why: EF Core’s DbContext already is a unit-of-work; a generic repository on top of it usually just renames Where() calls without adding real substitutability. I only introduce a repository interface when there’s an actual second implementation to swap in — see the S3 utility below, where the backing store legitimately varies.

decisions.choice: Five MediatR pipeline behaviours (validation, logging, performance, authorization, exception handling) ahead of every handler
decisions.instead: handling each concern inline, per handler
decisions.why: A new contributor adding an endpoint gets validation, logging, and auth enforcement for free, structurally, instead of relying on them remembering to add it. The cost is indirection — tracing a request means reading the pipeline, not just the handler, which is a real tradeoff on a small team.

publicRepos.name: S3 Storage
publicRepos.description: Layered S3 bucket/object API — the pattern behind the large-file ingestion pipeline I built at Global Holdings

layers.name: Infrastructure
layers.note: AWS SDK-backed implementation, mapped to Core DTOs

decisions.choice: Own response DTOs (CreateBucketResponse, etc.) instead of returning AWS SDK types up through the API
decisions.instead: passing PutBucketResponse and other SDK response objects straight through to callers
decisions.why: The AWS SDK’s response shapes change across major versions and carry AWS-specific metadata callers don’t need. Mapping at the Infrastructure boundary means an SDK upgrade is a one-file change, not an API contract break.

decisions.choice: Interface-driven IBucketRepository / IFilesRepository over the AWS SDK
decisions.instead: calling IAmazonS3 directly from the controllers
decisions.why: This is the case where the abstraction actually pays for itself: the object-storage backend legitimately varies — S3 here, a different cloud provider’s storage on the Global Holdings project — and the interface is what let me carry the same Core-layer contract across both without touching callers. If I only ever expected one provider for the life of a project, I’d skip this layer and call the SDK directly from a thin service.
